title: Does sublogarithmic randomized volume collapse to deterministic log-star?
formal: For every fixed locally checkable labeling problem Π on all bounded-degree graphs, does a randomized VOLUME algorithm with worst-case volume $o(\log(n+2))$ and global success probability at least 1−1/(n+1) imply a deterministic VOLUME algorithm with volume $O(1+\log^* n)$? The degree bound, checking radius, and finite input/output alphabets are fixed independently of n.
definitions: An LCL is a finite list of permitted rooted radius-r neighborhoods with input/output labels, degrees, and local ports, for fixed integers Δ≥2 and r≥1. All finite nonempty simple undirected graphs of maximum degree at most Δ, all input labels, all port orders, and all distinct identifiers from [|V(G)|²] are allowed; disconnected graphs are included. Legality depends on the finite neighborhoods, not on IDs or n. The query algorithm knows exact |V(G)| and starts at the requested vertex with its ID, degree, ports and input. It may follow any port of any visited vertex, revealing the next vertex and its local data; the visited set remains connected. Volume counts distinct visited vertices, including the queried one. Each graph vertex has its own independent infinite sequence of fair random bits, sampled once and used consistently by every query that visits it. A query may read finitely many bits from visited vertices, but has no access to a separate shared random tape. There is no preprocessing or mutable memory shared between queries. With probability at least 1−1/(|V(G)|+1), the answers to all vertex queries together must be a valid labeling. For a fixed algorithm A, V_A(n) is the maximum number of visited vertices over graphs of at most n vertices, all queries and all random tapes. Every computation must terminate; temporary space and local computation time are unrestricted. Both algorithms are uniform finite programs. log* is the number of iterated base-2 logarithms needed to reach at most 1.
answer_criterion: Prove the implication for every fixed LCL, or give one finite LCL specification with a sublogarithmic-volume randomized solver and prove that every deterministic solver fails every O(log* n) volume bound on arbitrarily large inputs. The known speedup below √log n makes deterministic and randomized O(log* n) equivalent for this purpose, so a counterexample would supply the missing intermediate randomized regime.
context:
A randomized local oracle can decide which parts of a graph to inspect using random choices. Its separate answers still need to fit together into one valid solution. The card samples one random tape per graph vertex and reuses it across queries, so an answer cannot evade an inconsistency by drawing fresh, unrelated randomness each time.

The cost is a worst-case information budget, with failure probability assigned to correctness. Bounding only the expected exploration size would be a different question. Likewise, success at one requested vertex is weaker than saying that all answers are simultaneously correct. These distinctions are significant when small failure probabilities are amplified across an entire graph.

There is already a strong speedup theorem: below √log n, randomized local computation can be replaced by deterministic O(log* n) computation. The conjectured threshold is log n. A candidate at, for example, (log n)^(3/4) would escape the existing theorem while remaining strictly below the proposed threshold.

Logarithmic randomized volume really occurs. The Lovász local lemma and sinkless orientation provide benchmark behavior at that scale in the cited work. The question is whether the whole interval immediately below log n is empty, beyond the familiar tiny-information symmetry-breaking regime.

Peng’s July 2026 constructions provide Θ((log n)^k) for positive integers k and polynomial scales up to polylogarithmic factors. Since the smallest exponent k is one, these do not insert a problem into the sublogarithmic interval. Figure 2 of that paper continues to mark the interval from √log n to log n as unknown.
why: A gap theorem would classify every sufficiently small randomized local computation as ordinary deterministic symmetry breaking. A counterexample would reveal a new scale of useful random exploration. This is a general complexity-landscape question, with consequences extending beyond any one coloring or matching algorithm.

importance.reason: An unresolved universal speedup threshold for randomized local computation. It isolates the remaining gap between a proven square-root-logarithmic threshold and the first established logarithmic examples.

progress.text: Rosenbaum and Suomela formalize randomized VOLUME with connected exploration and per-vertex random strings, and construct logarithmic and larger intermediate randomized complexities.

Brandt, Grunau, and Rozhoň prove the o(√log n) → deterministic O(log* n) speedup in Theorem 1.2. Their Conjecture 1.3 proposes the stronger o(log n) threshold for LCA; the VOLUME question considered here is explicitly tracked by later sources.
Suomela’s list asks whether an LCL can have randomized volume strictly between the log-star and logarithmic regimes.
Peng’s Theorem 1 fills the positive-integer polylogarithmic scales, and Theorem 2 gives rational polynomial exponents. Section 1.1 and Figure 2 retain the unknown interval from √log n to log n.
